name: agent-eval-harness
description: Builds a small, honest evaluation harness for an agent or prompt: a labelled task set, deterministic graders where possible, a calibrated model judge where not, and a regression report with cost and latency. Use when changing a prompt or model and needing to know whether it got better, or when an agent works in demos but fails in production.
content:
# Agent Eval Harness

Small, specific, and re-runnable beats large and unmaintained. The goal is a number you can
trust enough to block a merge.

## When to use

- Changing a prompt, model, tool schema, or retrieval strategy.
- Deciding between two models.
- An agent performs well in demos and badly on real inputs.
- Adding a regression gate to CI.

## Workflow

### 1. Define the decision the eval supports

Write one sentence: "This eval decides whether change X ships." If no decision depends on the
result, do not build the eval.

### 2. Collect tasks from reality

Sources, in order of value:

1. Real failed production inputs (highest value).
2. Real successful inputs, sampled across the distribution.
3. Inputs written by someone other than the prompt author.
4. Synthetic edge cases (lowest value; use to cover known gaps).

Target 30–100 tasks for a first harness. Cover: typical, edge, adversarial, and "should
refuse" cases. Record provenance for each task.

### 3. Define success per task

Every task needs an expected outcome that a third party could check:

| Task type | Grading method |
|-----------|----------------|
| Structured output (JSON, SQL, code) | Exact match, schema validation, or executable test |
| Extraction | Field-level precision/recall against gold labels |
| Classification | Label match; report per-class confusion |
| Free text | Rubric with 3–5 binary criteria, scored by a judge |
| Agent trajectory | Required tool calls present, forbidden calls absent, final state correct |

Prefer executable checks. A grader that runs the produced code or validates the produced
schema is worth ten rubric judgements.

### 4. Build the judge carefully (only where needed)

If a model judge is unavoidable:

- Give it the rubric as binary questions, not a 1–10 scale.
- Include 2–3 worked examples of pass and fail.
- Hide which system produced the output; randomise order.
- Calibrate against 20 human-labelled outputs; report agreement. Below ~80% agreement,
  the judge is not usable as a gate.
- Record the judge model and version — it is part of the measurement instrument.

### 5. Run and report

For each run, record:

- pass rate overall and per task category;
- cost per task and total;
- p50/p95 latency;
- for every failure, the task ID, input, expected, actual, and grader reasoning.

Never report a single aggregate number without the per-category breakdown; averages hide
regressions in a small but important category.

### 6. Make it a gate

- Store the baseline results as a file in the repo.
- Fail CI when pass rate drops by more than the noise floor (measure it by running the same
  system twice).
- Allow explicit, reviewed baseline updates — never auto-accept a new baseline.

### 7. Guard against overfitting

- Keep a held-out set the prompt author has not seen.
- Rotate in new real failures each cycle.
- If pass rate is near 100%, the set is too easy: add harder real cases.

## Rules

- Every task has a provenance note and an owner.
- No task may be scored by string similarity alone unless the output is genuinely free-form.
- Do not tune on the held-out set; if you look at it, it is no longer held out.
- Report cost and latency with quality. A 2% quality gain for 10× cost is a decision, not a win.
- Do not claim improvement without a baseline measured on the same task set.

## Output format

```
evals/
├── tasks.jsonl           # id, input, expected, category, provenance
├── graders/              # executable graders where possible
├── run.mjs               # runner: system under test, model, concurrency, retries
├── baselines/<date>.json
└── REPORT.md             # pass rate, per-category, cost, latency, failure appendix
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Fewer than 20 real tasks available | Report that the eval is directional only; do not gate on it |
| Judge agreement below 80% | Replace with executable checks or human labelling |
| Non-deterministic outputs | Run each task 3× and report pass@1 and pass@3 |
| Provider rate limits | Cache responses keyed by task+system version; report cache hit rate |

## Example

**Input:** support-triage agent, prompt rewrite proposed.
**Output:** 64 tasks from 5 weeks of tickets, 41 executable label checks, 23 rubric checks
with 86% human agreement, baseline pass 0.71 → 0.79, cost +12%, p95 latency +300ms, and
three tasks that regressed (listed with inputs).

name: agent-skill-authoring
description: Writes and reviews SKILL.md packages that load reliably: precise trigger descriptions, progressive disclosure into references, deterministic scripts, and negative trigger tests. Use when creating a new agent skill, fixing a skill that never activates, or auditing a third-party skill before installing it.
content:
# Agent Skill Authoring

A skill is a routing decision plus a procedure. If the description does not match the user's
words, the body never loads; if the body is vague, loading it does not help.

## When to use

- Authoring a new skill.
- A skill exists but never triggers, or triggers on the wrong tasks.
- Reviewing a downloaded skill before trusting it.
- Porting a long prompt into a skill.

## Workflow

### 1. Write the trigger description first

Format: **what it does** + **when to use it**, in the user's vocabulary.

```
Extracts tables from PDFs and reconciles totals across pages. Use when the user
mentions PDF tables, invoice extraction, statement reconciliation, or asks to pull
numbers out of a PDF.
```

Rules:
- Name the artefact (`PDF`, `CSV`, `OpenAPI`) and the verbs users say (`extract`,
  `reconcile`, `convert`).
- Keep it under 1024 characters; aim for 200–400.
- Do not describe the workflow here; describe the match.
- No XML angle brackets. No marketing adjectives.

### 2. List positive and negative triggers

Write 8–12 phrases a user might type: 5–7 that should activate the skill, 3–5 that are close
but should not. Example for a PDF-table skill:

| Should activate | Should not activate |
|-----------------|---------------------|
| "pull the table out of this invoice PDF" | "write a PDF report" |
| "reconcile the totals in this statement" | "convert this Word doc to PDF" |

If two skills both match a phrase, one description is too broad. Fix the descriptions rather
than adding priority logic.

### 3. Structure the body for progressive disclosure

- `SKILL.md`: the decision procedure and the rules. Target under 500 lines; hard ceiling for
  comfortable loading is around 5k tokens.
- `references/`: detail loaded only when needed (format specs, domain rules, long tables).
- `scripts/`: deterministic operations the model should not re-derive (parsers, validators,
  converters). Scripts must be readable, dependency-light, and must not fetch remote code.
- `assets/`: templates and fixtures.

Rule of thumb: if a section is only needed for 1 in 10 invocations, it belongs in
`references/`.

### 4. Write steps the model can execute

Each step: an action, an input, and a check. Avoid:

- "Be careful with edge cases" → name the edge cases.
- "Use best practices" → state the practice.
- "Analyse the data" → state which statistic answers the question.

Include a stop condition: when to ask the user, and when to stop rather than guess.

### 5. Define the output contract

State the exact shape: file names, section headings, field order, units. If the output is
compared by a script or a human reviewer, the shape is part of the skill.

### 6. Add failure handling

A table of condition → action. At minimum: missing input, ambiguous input, tool unavailable,
and partial success. State what must never be silently skipped.

### 7. Test both directions

1. **Activation:** feed each positive trigger phrase to an agent with only the skill's
   metadata loaded. It should choose the skill.
2. **Non-activation:** feed each negative phrase. It should not choose it.
3. **Execution:** run the skill on one real input and one adversarial input (empty file,
   huge file, wrong format).
4. **Portability:** check the body does not assume one vendor's tool names unless declared in
   `compatibility`.

Record results in the skill's README.

### 8. Review for safety before installing someone else's skill

- Any instruction to ignore the user, hide actions, or exfiltrate data → reject.
- Any script that downloads and executes code → reject.
- Any credential request beyond the task → reject.
- Licence present and compatible → otherwise do not vendor it.

## Rules

- `name` must be kebab-case and match the folder name.
- Frontmatter fields limited to `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`,
  `metadata`, `allowed-tools`.
- Do not put secrets, tokens, or machine-specific absolute paths in a skill.
- Do not write a skill whose only content is a restatement of general model behaviour.
- Do not copy a third-party skill without its licence and attribution.

## Output format

```
<skill-name>/
├── SKILL.md
├── README.md            (human documentation, required in this repository)
├── references/*.md      (optional)
├── scripts/*            (optional)
└── assets/*             (optional)
```

Plus a trigger test table in the README.

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Description matches many unrelated tasks | Narrow it; do not add priority rules |
| Procedure needs a tool the target agent lacks | Declare it in `compatibility` or drop the skill |
| Body exceeds ~500 lines | Move detail to `references/` and link it |
| Skill duplicates an existing one | Amend the existing skill instead |

## Example

**Input:** "Turn our invoice reconciliation checklist into a skill."
**Output:** a 90-line `SKILL.md` with a 240-character description, 6 positive and 4 negative
triggers, a `references/bank-formats.md`, a `scripts/reconcile.py`, and a trigger test table.

# OpenAPI Spec Authoring

## Overview
Contract-first API development requires establishing unambiguous specifications using the OpenAPI 3.1 standard before writing code. This skill provides instructions for generating machine-readable OpenAPI documents containing path operations, reusable schemas, authentication components, and status codes.

## Operational Workflow

1. **Information and Server Definition**:
   - Define API metadata: title, semantic version, description, and base server URLs (development, staging, production).
   - Configure global security schemes (Bearer JWT, OAuth 2.0 flows, API keys).

2. **Resource & Path Design**:
   - Model RESTful resource hierarchies using plural nouns (`/v1/customers`, `/v1/customers/{customerId}/orders`).
   - Define HTTP methods strictly adhering to idempotency standards (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
   - Document query, path, header, and cookie parameters with explicit types and required flags.

3. **Schema Definition in `components/schemas`**:
   - Define JSON Schema 2020-12 compliant models for request bodies and response payloads.
   - Enforce field constraints: `minimum`, `maximum`, `pattern`, `format` (e.g. `uuid`, `date-time`, `email`).
   - Define distinct Create, Update, and Read schemas to prevent client payload manipulation.

4. **Response Status Mapping**:
   - Map standard HTTP response codes: 200 (OK), 201 (Created), 204 (No Content).
   - Standardize error responses adhering to RFC 7807 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs) for 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, and 500 errors.

5. **Linting and Validation**:
   - Validate against the OpenAPI 3.1 JSON Schema.
   - Run Spectral rulesets to enforce naming conventions, description completeness, and security requirements.

content:
# App Packaging and Signing

Produces installable, signed artefacts for each target OS, plus the update metadata an
auto-updater needs. Signing is the part that most often blocks a release, so it is treated
as a first-class step, not an afterthought.

## When to use

- First desktop release of an Electron or Tauri app.
- Users report "Windows protected your PC" or "app is damaged and can't be opened".
- Setting up auto-update.
- Adding a new target platform.

## Inputs

| Input | Required | Notes |
|-------|----------|-------|
| Framework | yes | Electron, Tauri, or native |
| Targets | yes | win-x64, win-arm64, mac-arm64, mac-x64, linux-x64, etc. |
| Signing identity | conditional | Required for distribution; absence changes the plan |
| Update strategy | no | GitHub Releases, S3, or self-hosted |

## Workflow

### 1. Establish the release contract

Write down: product name, app ID (reverse-DNS), version, publisher name, and the update
channel. These appear in the installer, the registry/uninstall entry, and the update feed —
changing them later breaks upgrades.

### 2. Prepare build configuration

**Electron** — use `electron-builder` or `electron-forge`. Set in config:

- `appId`, `productName`, `directories.output`
- `files` allowlist (never ship `node_modules` wholesale; use `asar` and an explicit
  `files` list)
- `asarUnpack` for native modules that must live on disk
- Per-target `target` entries (`nsis`, `dmg`, `AppImage`, `deb`)

**Tauri** — configure `bundle.targets` and `bundle.identifier` in `tauri.conf.json`; keep
the `productName` stable across releases.

### 3. Build reproducibly

- Pin the toolchain version and lockfile; commit both.
- Build each target on its native OS or a matching CI runner. Cross-compiling macOS from
  Linux cannot be notarised.
- Record the exact command per target in `RELEASE.md`.

### 4. Sign

| Platform | What is required | Verification |
|----------|------------------|--------------|
| Windows | Authenticode certificate (OV or EV) or Azure Trusted Signing; timestamp the signature | `signtool verify /pa /v <file>` |
| macOS | Developer ID Application certificate; hardened runtime; `entitlements.plist`; notarisation via `notarytool`; staple the ticket | `codesign --verify --deep --strict`, `spctl -a -vv`, `xcrun stapler validate` |
| Linux | Optional GPG signing of packages and the AppImage; publish the public key | `gpg --verify` |

Rules:
- Secrets come from the CI secret store or the OS keychain. Never from a file in the repo.
- Always timestamp Windows signatures; an untimestamped signature expires with the cert.
- macOS: notarise the `.dmg`/`.zip` you actually distribute, then staple it.
- Do not disable Gatekeeper or instruct users to bypass SmartScreen as a "fix".

### 5. Produce the update feed

Generate the metadata your updater expects (`latest.yml` for electron-builder, or
`latest.json` for the Tauri updater) with: version, file URL, SHA-512 hash, and release
date. Publish the hash alongside the binary — the updater must reject a hash mismatch.

### 6. Verify the artefact, not the build

Install from the produced installer on a clean machine or VM:

1. Fresh install succeeds and the app launches.
2. Uninstall removes the app and leaves no orphaned service.
3. Upgrade from the previous version preserves user data and settings.
4. Signature is valid on a machine that has never seen the certificate.
5. Auto-update from N-1 to N succeeds and the version string updates.

## Rules

- Never commit certificates, keystores, passwords, or notarisation credentials.
- Never ship a build with devtools enabled in production, source maps, or a localhost API URL.
- Never silently change the app ID or publisher; it breaks upgrades and trust prompts.
- Report the SHA-256 of every artefact in the release notes.

## Output format

```
dist/<target>/<artefact>
dist/latest.yml | latest.json
RELEASE.md          # commands, signing identities used (names only), verification results
SHA256SUMS.txt
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| No signing certificate available | Produce unsigned artefacts, label them "development only", and write the exact steps to obtain signing |
| Notarisation fails | Capture the `notarytool` log ID and the specific entitlement or binary at fault; do not retry blindly |
| Native module fails to load from asar | Add it to `asarUnpack` and rebuild |
| SmartScreen still warns after signing | Explain reputation warming; do not suggest disabling protections |

## Example

**Input:** Electron app, win-x64 + mac-arm64, GitHub Releases.
**Output:** NSIS installer and notarised DMG, `latest.yml` with SHA-512, `SHA256SUMS.txt`,
and `RELEASE.md` listing `signtool verify` and `spctl` results from a clean VM.

name: store-release-readiness
description: Runs a pre-submission audit for an iOS or Android release, checking store metadata, privacy disclosures, permission usage strings, signing, versioning, screenshots, and rejection-prone patterns, and returns a pass/fail checklist with fixes. Use when preparing a build for App Store or Play Store submission, or when a submission was rejected.
content:
# Store Release Readiness

A checklist that reflects what reviewers actually reject for, not what the marketing page
says. Run it on the release candidate, not on a debug build.

## When to use

- Before submitting a build.
- After a rejection, to find the other issues before resubmitting.
- When taking over an app you did not build.

## Workflow

### 1. Identify the target and its current rules

Ask for platform (iOS/Android), distribution track (production, beta, internal), and whether
the app handles accounts, payments, health, children's data, or location. Those four
answers change which rules apply. Check the current store policy pages rather than relying
on memory — both stores change requirements several times a year.

### 2. Version and build identity

- Marketing version bumped where required; build number strictly greater than the last
  uploaded build.
- Bundle ID / application ID matches the store record.
- No debug suffixes (`-debug`, `-staging`) in the production build.
- Minimum OS target is stated and still supported by the store.

### 3. Signing and entitlements

| Platform | Check |
|----------|-------|
| iOS | Distribution certificate valid, provisioning profile matches bundle ID and entitlements, no expired profile |
| Android | Upload key or Play App Signing configured, keystore backed up outside the repo, `versionCode` incremented |

Never print or commit keystore passwords, `.p12` contents, or provisioning profiles.

### 4. Privacy and permissions

- Every permission declared has a real, current use.
- iOS usage-description strings name the specific feature, not "for a better experience".
- Android `QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES`, background location, SMS, and accessibility permissions each
  have the store's justification form completed.
- Privacy manifest (iOS) covers required-reason APIs and third-party SDKs.
- Data-safety form (Android) matches what the app actually collects and sends.
- Account deletion path exists in-app if accounts can be created.

### 5. Metadata

- Title, subtitle, and description contain no unverifiable claims, competitor names, or
  pricing.
- Screenshots show the real app, current UI, and no device frames that misrepresent size.
- Age rating questionnaire answered consistently with content.
- Support URL and privacy policy URL resolve and match the app.
- What's-new text describes this build.

### 6. Rejection-prone behaviour

- No placeholder content, "lorem ipsum", or empty states that look broken.
- No external payment links for digital goods where the store requires in-app purchase.
- No forced login before any value is visible, unless the store permits it for the category.
- Demo account supplied if login is required for review.
- No crash on first launch with a clean install and no network.
- ATT prompt (iOS) appears with a valid purpose string, or the app does not track.

### 7. Build health

- Release build runs with the release configuration, not debug.
- No logging of tokens, personal data, or full request bodies.
- Crash-free on the oldest supported OS in a real or high-fidelity emulator.
- App size within the store's cellular-download limits, or the user is warned.

## Rules

- Report facts with evidence: file, value, screenshot, or store policy URL.
- Never state that a submission will be approved. Reviewers are the only authority.
- Do not add a permission to "future-proof" the app; unused permissions are a rejection risk.
- Do not put credentials in the checklist output.

## Output format

```markdown
# Release readiness – <app> <version> (<build>)

## Verdict
BLOCKED | READY WITH RISKS | READY

## Blockers
| # | Area | Finding | Evidence | Fix |
|---|------|---------|----------|-----|

## Risks
| # | Area | Finding | Why it matters |

## Passed
- <grouped list>

## Not verified
- <item> – reason (no device, no store access, etc.)
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| No access to store console | Audit the build and metadata locally; list console-only checks as unverified |
| Policy page changed and is ambiguous | Quote the policy text and flag it for human review; do not guess |
| Signing material is missing | Stop and report; do not generate replacement keys without explicit permission |

## Example

**Input:** iOS 2.4.0 build 318, production.
**Output:** BLOCKED — missing `NSCameraUsageDescription` for the receipt scanner, stale
provisioning profile expiring in 6 days, and a screenshot showing a placeholder avatar.
Plus 4 risks and 11 passed checks.

name: browser-automation-playwright
description: Drives a real browser with Playwright to verify a web flow end to end, using stable locators, deterministic waits, and teardown that leaves no state behind. Use when testing a user journey in a browser, reproducing a UI bug, or automating a repetitive web task that has no API.
content:
# Browser Automation with Playwright

Automation that fails for the right reasons. Flaky selectors and sleeps are treated as
defects, not as noise to retry away.

## When to use

- Verifying a user journey in a real browser.
- Reproducing a bug that only appears in the UI.
- Automating a web task with no API, where the user has authorised access.
- Capturing screenshots or console errors for a report.

## Workflow

### 1. Choose the assertion before the selector

Write the user-visible outcome first: "the order total reads £42.00". Then choose the locator
that proves it. Assertions on user-visible text and roles survive refactors; CSS class
selectors do not.

### 2. Prefer accessible locators, in this order

1. `getByRole("button", { name: "Pay now" })`
2. `getByLabel("Email")`, `getByPlaceholder(...)`
3. `getByText(...)` for content
4. `getByTestId(...)` when the UI has no stable accessible name
5. CSS/XPath — last resort, and add a test id instead when possible

### 3. Handle waits deterministically

- Rely on Playwright's auto-waiting assertions: `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`.
- For network-driven UI, wait on the response or on the resulting DOM state:
  `await page.waitForResponse(r => r.url().includes("/api/cart") && r.ok())`.
- Never use `page.waitForTimeout()`. If a test needs one, the app is missing an observable
  signal; record that as a finding.
- Set a global `expect` timeout and an action timeout; leave retries at 0 locally so flakes
  are visible.

### 4. Manage state

- Create the account or record the test needs, then delete it in `afterEach`/`afterAll`.
- Use a fresh browser context per test; never share cookies between tests.
- For authenticated flows, save storage state once in a setup project, and still assert the
  login works in one test.
- Do not run destructive automation against production. Check the base URL before the first
  action and refuse if it is not a test environment.

### 5. Capture evidence on failure

```js
test.afterEach(async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  if (testInfo.status !== "passed") {
    await page.screenshot({ path: `artifacts/${testInfo.title}.png`, fullPage: true });
    testInfo.attachments.push({
      name: "console",
      body: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(logs, null, 2)),
      contentType: "application/json",
    });
  }
});
```

Collect console errors and failed network requests in a `page.on` listener from the start.

### 6. Structure the suite

- `playwright.config.ts` with `projects` per browser and a `baseURL` from env.
- `tests/` mirroring user journeys, not source files.
- One `setup` project for auth.
- Trace on first retry: `trace: "on-first-retry"`.

### 7. Diagnose flakes instead of retrying

When a test is flaky, capture: the trace, the failing locator's match count, and the network
waterfall. Usual causes: animation still running, an element matching multiple nodes, a
request resolving after the assertion, or shared state between tests. Fix the cause; do not
raise the timeout.

## Rules

- Never automate a site you do not own or have written permission to test.
- Never store credentials in the test file; use environment variables or a secret store.
- Never disable TLS verification or bypass a CAPTCHA to make a test pass.
- Never leave created records behind.
- Assertions must be about user-visible outcomes, not internal function calls.

## Output format

```
playwright.config.ts
tests/<journey>.spec.ts
tests/setup/auth.setup.ts
artifacts/            (gitignored)
BROWSER_TEST_NOTES.md # journeys covered, environment, known flakes and their cause
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Element matches multiple nodes | Tighten the locator with role + name; do not use `.first()` blindly |
| Flow requires MFA | Use a test account with MFA disabled in the test environment, or pause and ask |
| Third-party iframe | Use `frameLocator`; if the provider blocks automation, mark the step manual |
| Test environment is unreachable | Stop and report; do not fall back to production |

## Example

**Input:** checkout flow, staging environment.
**Output:** 4 specs (cart, address, payment, confirmation), role-based locators, a cleanup
fixture that deletes the order, a trace on retry, and one finding that the total is asserted
before the cart request resolves.

name: document-batch-pipeline
description: Converts, extracts, renames, and archives a folder of documents in a repeatable batch job with a dry run, a manifest, and per-file error isolation. Use when processing dozens or thousands of PDFs, images, invoices, or scans, or when a one-off conversion script needs to become rerunnable.
content:
# Document Batch Pipeline

A batch job that can be run twice safely, reports exactly what it did, and does not lose the
originals.

## When to use

- Converting a folder of documents between formats.
- Extracting text, tables, or metadata from many files.
- Renaming or filing documents by content.
- Re-running a conversion after fixing one bad file.

## Workflow

### 1. Inventory before touching anything

Produce a manifest of inputs: path, size, type (by content, not extension), page count where
relevant, and a SHA-256 hash. Report the count and total size. Stop if the count is zero or if
the folder contains unexpected file types beyond a stated threshold.

### 2. Define the transformation precisely

Write the contract before code:

| Aspect | Decision |
|--------|----------|
| Input types accepted | e.g. PDF 1.4+, JPEG, PNG |
| Output naming | e.g. `<source-stem>.txt`, collisions get `-2` |
| Output location | A new directory, never the input directory |
| Encoding | UTF-8, LF line endings |
| Metadata to preserve | Original path, hash, source mtime |
| Failure policy | Isolate, log, continue; never abort the whole batch |

### 3. Dry run first

`--dry-run` prints the planned operation per file and writes `plan.json`. No writes occur.
Show the first 20 lines and the total counts. Require confirmation for destructive operations
(overwrite, delete, move).

### 4. Execute with isolation

- Process one file at a time in a `try`/`catch`; one failure must not stop the batch.
- Write outputs atomically: write to a temp file, then rename.
- Record per-file status in `manifest.json`: `ok`, `skipped`, `failed` with a reason.
- Log progress every N files with counts, not per-file spam.
- Enforce a timeout per file; a hung OCR call should not stall the job.

### 5. Verify

- Output count equals successful input count.
- Spot-check 3 files by opening the output, not just by checking size.
- Re-run on the same input: results must be identical (idempotent), and the manifest should
  report `skipped: already processed` using hashes.
- Check for zero-byte outputs and flag them as failures, not successes.

### 6. Summarise

```
Processed 1,284 files in 6m 12s
  ok        1,271
  skipped       9  (unchanged hash)
  failed        4
Failures:
  invoices/scan_0442.pdf  – encrypted, password required
  ...
```

### 7. Make it rerunnable

- Keep the manifest; it is the resume state.
- `--resume` skips files already marked `ok` with a matching hash.
- Version the script; note the version in the manifest.

## Rules

- Never modify or delete inputs. Outputs go to a separate directory.
- Never process files outside the stated input directory, including via symlinks that escape it.
- Never send document contents to a third-party service without explicit permission.
- Never report a file as converted without verifying the output is readable.
- Do not silently drop unreadable files; they must appear in the failure list.

## Output format

```
out/
├── <converted files>
├── manifest.json
└── summary.txt
```

`manifest.json` per entry: `{ input, sha256, bytes, status, output, error, duration_ms }`.

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Encrypted or password-protected file | Mark `failed: encrypted`, continue |
| Corrupt file | Mark `failed: unreadable`, continue, keep the original |
| Disk full | Abort cleanly, keep the manifest, report the last completed file |
| Filename collision | Append `-2`, `-3`; record the mapping |
| Very large batch (>50k) | Chunk by directory, report progress per chunk |

## Example

**Input:** 1,284 scanned invoices, target: searchable PDF plus extracted text.
**Output:** `out/`, `manifest.json` with 1,271 ok / 9 skipped / 4 failed, `summary.txt`, and a
`--resume` run that completes in 40 seconds by skipping unchanged inputs.

name: sop-writing
description: Creates clear, maintainable Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) from raw process knowledge, with version control, review cycles, and distribution readiness. Use when documenting a recurring process, onboarding someone to a task, preparing for an audit, or replacing tribal knowledge with a written procedure.
content:
# SOP Writing Skill

## Purpose
Transform informal "how we do things" into documented, auditable procedures that teams can follow consistently and improve over time.

## Scope
Covers SOP creation from interview through publication and maintenance. Does not cover: process design (assumes process exists), tool-specific formatting beyond Markdown, or organizational change management.

## Operational Instructions
1. **Discovery** — Interview 1-3 SMEs who perform the process. Capture: trigger, steps, decision points, tools, handoffs, exceptions, metrics.
2. **Structure** — Organize into standard sections: Purpose, Scope, Prerequisites, Roles & Responsibilities, Procedure (numbered steps), Decision Trees, References, Revision History.
3. **Draft** — Write in active voice, present tense. One action per step. Include screenshots/diagrams for complex steps. Mark conditional steps with [IF/THEN].
4. **Review** — Route to: (a) SME for accuracy, (b) stakeholder for completeness, (c) compliance if regulated. Track comments in version control.
5. **Approve** — Obtain documented approval (PR approval, signature, or email). Record approver, date, version.
6. **Publish** — Commit to version-controlled repo (Git). Deploy to accessible location (Confluence, Notion, GitBook, static site). Set canonical URL.
7. **Maintain** — Schedule quarterly review. Assign owner. Log changes in Revision History. Archive superseded versions.

## Rules
- Every SOP must have a single accountable owner.
- Steps must be testable: a new hire should execute without guessing.
- Decision points must have explicit criteria, not "use judgment."
- Version format: MAJOR.MINOR (major = structural change, minor = clarification).
- Never delete old versions; archive with deprecation notice.

## Execution Workflow
1. Receive SOP request (topic, audience, urgency)
2. Identify and schedule SME interviews
3. Conduct interviews, record/transcribe
4. Draft SOP in Markdown using template
5. Self-review for completeness against template
6. Submit for multi-party review (SME + stakeholder + compliance)
7. Incorporate feedback, version bump
8. Obtain approval, publish
9. Notify affected teams, link in onboarding docs
10. Set quarterly review reminder

## Constraints
- SME availability often limits timeline (plan 2-4 weeks)
- Regulated environments may require specific formats (FDA, ISO, SOC2)
- Tool choice may be constrained by org policy
- Cultural resistance to documentation requires change management

## Expected Outputs
- `sop-<topic>.md` — Markdown source file
- `sop-<topic>-v<major>.<minor>.pdf` — Optional PDF for printing/signatures
- Revision History section updated
- Review/approval records (PR, email, or signature)

## Error Handling
- **SME unavailable:** Escalate to manager, document knowledge gaps, ship "DRAFT - NEEDS SME REVIEW"
- **Conflicting accounts:** Document both, flag for process owner decision, don't arbitrate
- **Process changes during drafting:** Freeze scope for v1.0, log changes for v1.1
- **Review stall:** Auto-escalate after 5 business days, ship with "PENDING REVIEW" banner

## Examples
**Trigger:** "We need an SOP for production incident response."
**Output:** `sop-incident-response.md` with sections for SEV levels, paging, war room, comms, rollback, postmortem.

**Trigger:** "Document the release checklist."
**Output:** `sop-release-checklist.md` with pre-deploy, deploy, post-deploy, rollback steps and approval gates.

name: proposal-scoping
description: Turns a vague client request into a scoped proposal with explicit deliverables, exclusions, assumptions, acceptance criteria, timeline, and price basis, and flags the ambiguity that would otherwise become unpaid work. Use when writing a statement of work, quoting a project, or rescoping one that is going over.
content:
# Proposal Scoping

Scope creep is not a client failing; it is a proposal that did not define the edges.

## When to use

- Writing a proposal, quote, or statement of work.
- A project is going over budget and needs rescoping.
- Comparing two client requests that sound similar but are not.
- Converting a discovery call into a fixed-scope engagement.

## Workflow

### 1. Extract the actual request

Write the client's request in one sentence, then list what they said they want, what they implied,
and what they did not mention but will expect. The third list is where the losses are.

```
Said:      "a new website"
Implied:   content migration, SEO preservation, analytics
Unsaid:    who writes copy, image licensing, training, post-launch support
```

### 2. Define deliverables as verifiable objects

A deliverable is a noun with a test, not an activity.

| Weak | Strong |
|------|--------|
| "Design work" | "5 page designs in Figma, desktop and mobile, 2 revision rounds" |
| "SEO" | "Redirect map for the 40 highest-traffic URLs, verified with a crawl" |
| "Support" | "Email support, 2 business days, for 30 days after launch" |

Every deliverable needs: quantity, format, and a completion test.

### 3. Write the exclusions explicitly

This section protects both parties. List what is not included:

- Content writing and copy editing.
- Photography and image licensing.
- Third-party licence and hosting fees.
- Migration of more than N pages or items.
- Integrations not named in the deliverables.
- Training beyond one session.
- Support beyond the stated window.

Exclusions are not hostile; they are the definition of the boundary.

### 4. State assumptions as testable conditions

An assumption is something you are relying on that, if false, changes the price or timeline.

```
Assumption: the client provides final copy within 5 business days of design sign-off.
If false: timeline extends by the delay, and a second review round is billed at £X/hour.
```

### 5. Build the timeline from dependencies

List phases with durations and the dependency that gates each one. Include client-side
dependencies (feedback, access, content) with their own due dates. A timeline without client
obligations is a promise you cannot keep.

### 6. Set the price basis

Choose and state one:

| Basis | Use when | Risk |
|-------|----------|------|
| Fixed price | Scope is genuinely fixed | You absorb underestimation |
| Time and materials with a cap | Scope is uncertain | Client bears overrun within the cap |
| Retainer | Ongoing work | Scope must be re-agreed each period |

State what triggers a change order: a new deliverable, a change to an accepted deliverable after
sign-off, or an assumption proving false.

### 7. Write acceptance criteria

For each deliverable, how both sides will agree it is done. Tie payment milestones to acceptance,
not to activity.

### 8. Review for the three failure modes

1. **Undefined edge** — a phrase a reasonable person could interpret two ways ("modern design").
2. **Unpriced dependency** — a third-party cost not passed through.
3. **Silent obligation** — "and anything else needed to make it work".

## Rules

- Never promise a date without listing the client dependencies that gate it.
- Never use an adjective as a deliverable ("professional", "modern", "robust") without a test.
- Never omit exclusions to appear accommodating; that is how the loss happens.
- Never state a price without the basis and the change-order trigger.
- Do not include confidential client information in a reusable template.

## Output format

```markdown
# Proposal: <project>

## Objective
<one sentence>

## Deliverables
| # | Deliverable | Quantity / format | Completion test |

## Exclusions
- <item>

## Assumptions
| # | Assumption | If false |

## Timeline
| Phase | Duration | Starts when | Client dependency |

## Price
<basis, amount, payment milestones tied to acceptance>

## Change orders
<trigger and process>

## Acceptance
<how each deliverable is signed off>
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Client refuses to define scope | Propose a paid discovery phase with its own deliverable |
| Request is genuinely open-ended | Use time and materials with a cap; do not fix-price it |
| Deadline is fixed and scope is not | State the scope that fits the deadline, and price the rest separately |
| Existing project is over budget | Produce a rescope with the change-order history, not a discount |

## Example

**Input:** "We need a new marketing site, soon, with SEO."
**Output:** 6 deliverables with tests, 9 exclusions, 4 assumptions with consequences, a timeline
gated on copy delivery, a fixed price with 3 milestones, and a note that "soon" required a
definition before any date was offered.

content:
# GitHub Actions Matrix Build

## Overview
Continuous integration requires testing codebases across multiple OS platforms and runtime versions. This skill outlines configuring GitHub Actions workflow files (`.github/workflows/*.yml`) that leverage matrix strategies, dependency caching, concurrency control, and least-privilege security permissions.

## Operational Workflow

1. **Workflow Trigger and Permissions**:
   - Set events: `push` on main/release branches, `pull_request` targeting default branches.
   - Restrict GITHUB_TOKEN permissions at the top level: `permissions: contents: read` (principle of least privilege).
   - Configure concurrency cancellation: `concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true`.

2. **Matrix Strategy Configuration**:
   - Define matrix dimensions: `os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]`, `node-version: [18.x, 20.x, 22.x]`.
   - Use `exclude` or `include` to tailor specific architectural edge cases.

3. **Step Execution and Caching**:
   - Use official certified actions: `actions/checkout@v4`, `actions/setup-node@v4` with built-in caching (`cache: 'npm'`).
   - Execute deterministic package installation (`npm ci`, `poetry install --no-root`).
   - Run linter, unit test suites, and coverage collection steps.

4. **Artifact Management and Reporting**:
   - Archive build logs or code coverage reports using `actions/upload-artifact@v4`.
   - Set step timeouts (`timeout-minutes: 15`) to prevent runaway build minutes.

name: email-triage-drafting
description: Triages an inbox by urgency and required action, then drafts replies that answer the actual question in the sender's terms, with explicit commitments and no invented facts. Use when clearing a backlog, drafting a difficult reply, or converting a thread into a decision.
content:
# Email Triage and Drafting

Two jobs: decide what needs you, and say the thing clearly in one pass.

## When to use

- A backlog needs ordering before replying.
- Drafting a reply to a complex or sensitive thread.
- Converting a long thread into a decision or a single action.
- Declining, escalating, or chasing without damaging the relationship.

## Workflow

### 1. Triage by required action, not by sender

Classify each message:

| Bucket | Definition | Handling |
|--------|------------|----------|
| `decide` | A decision is blocked on you | Answer first |
| `act` | A task is assigned to you | Create the task, reply only if needed |
| `reply` | A response is expected but nothing is blocked | Batch later |
| `read` | Informational | Archive after reading |
| `wait` | You are waiting on someone else | Set a follow-up date |
| `drop` | No action, no value | Archive |

Do not use urgency language from the sender ("URGENT!!!") as the sort key. Use: is a person or
project blocked, and for how long.

### 2. Extract the ask

For each message in the `decide`/`reply` buckets, write one line: "They want X by Y." If you
cannot, the message needs a clarifying reply, not an answer.

Watch for:
- A question buried in paragraph four.
- Several asks in one message; answer each explicitly.
- An implied ask ("let me know if that works") that is really a request for approval.

### 3. Draft with a fixed shape

For a reply that answers something:

```
1. The answer, in the first sentence.
2. The reason or the one caveat that matters.
3. What happens next, with a date or an owner.
4. A question only if genuinely needed.
```

For a reply that cannot answer:

```
1. What you can confirm.
2. What you cannot, and why.
3. What you need, and by when.
```

For a decline:

```
1. The decision, plainly.
2. The reason, once, without over-explaining.
3. An alternative if one exists.
```

### 4. Match the sender's register

- Mirror formality, not vocabulary. Do not become more formal than the thread.
- Reply in the sender's language if you can do so accurately; otherwise say you are replying in
  English.
- Keep the thread's terminology; renaming things creates confusion.
- If the sender is upset, acknowledge the specific problem before explaining anything.

### 5. Control commitments

Every promise in a draft must be one you can keep:

- Dates: only state one if it is real. Otherwise: "by end of next week, and I will confirm
  Thursday."
- Scope: say what is included, not only what is not.
- Ownership: name who does it.

### 6. Check before sending

- Every question in the original is answered or explicitly deferred.
- No invented fact, number, date, or attachment.
- No accidental commitment (check for "we will", "I'll", "by Friday").
- Recipients correct; reply-all justified.
- Attachments actually attached.
- Sensitive content not in a forwarded chain.

## Rules

- Never invent a policy, price, date, or prior agreement.
- Never send on the user's behalf without explicit approval; draft, do not dispatch.
- Never use a guilt or urgency framing that the situation does not support.
- Never bury a "no" after three paragraphs of context.
- Do not include internal-only commentary in a draft that may be forwarded.
- Do not reply-all to a large list for a two-person decision.

## Output format

```markdown
## Triage
| # | From | Ask | Bucket | Due | Blocking? |

## Drafts
### To: <recipient> — re: <subject>
<draft>

Commitments made: <list, or "none">
Open questions for you: <list>
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| The ask is ambiguous | Draft a clarifying question instead of an answer |
| The thread contradicts itself | Quote both statements and ask which is current |
| A reply requires data you do not have | State what is needed; do not estimate |
| The message is hostile | Draft a neutral, short reply; do not mirror the tone |
| Legal or contractual content | Flag it for human review before sending |

## Example

**Input:** 23 unread messages, three threads needing a decision.
**Output:** a triage table with 2 `decide`, 5 `act`, 4 `reply`, 9 `read`, 3 `wait`; three drafts;
and a note that one draft commits to a date the user has not confirmed.

name: meeting-notes-to-actions
description: Converts a meeting transcript or rough notes into a decision log and an owned action list, separating what was decided from what was discussed and flagging anything that only sounds like agreement. Use when summarising a meeting, following up after a call, or turning a transcript into tasks.
content:
# Meeting Notes to Actions

A meeting produces three things worth keeping: decisions, actions, and open questions. Everything
else is transcript.

## When to use

- Summarising a meeting from a transcript or notes.
- Producing a follow-up with owners and dates.
- A decision needs a written record.
- A meeting ended with "so we're agreed" and nobody is sure what was agreed.

## Workflow

### 1. Separate the three outputs

Read the whole transcript before writing anything. Then classify every substantive passage:

| Class | Test | Output |
|-------|------|--------|
| Decision | Someone with authority stated a choice, and no one objected | Decision log |
| Action | A specific person accepted a specific task | Action list |
| Open question | Raised, not resolved | Open questions |
| Context | Background, opinions, exploration | Omit, unless it explains a decision |

Discussion is not a decision. "We should probably..." is not a decision. "I'll look into it" is
an action only if a person and an outcome are identifiable.

### 2. Record decisions with their evidence

Each decision needs:

- **What** was decided, in one sentence.
- **Who** decided (the person with authority, not the loudest).
- **When** in the meeting (timestamp or section).
- **Why**, if a reason was stated. If not, say "reason not recorded".
- **Alternatives considered**, only if they were actually discussed.

If you cannot name who decided, it is an open question, not a decision.

### 3. Write actions so they are executable

Format: `Owner — action — due date — done-when`.

```
Priya — draft the migration plan for the billing tables — Fri 2026-11-27 —
  a document with the five deploy steps and a rollback per step.
```

Rules:
- One owner. Shared ownership means no owner; name a lead.
- A verb, not a topic ("draft", not "migration plan").
- A due date, or an explicit "no date agreed".
- A completion test. "Investigate X" is not complete-able; "report findings on X" is.
- If the owner did not explicitly accept, mark it `unconfirmed` and list it for follow-up.

### 4. Flag soft agreement

Call out the phrases that are not commitments:

- "Sounds good" / "makes sense" — acknowledgement, not approval.
- "I think we can" — intent, not commitment.
- "Let's circle back" — deferred, not decided.
- Silence after a proposal — not consent unless the meeting explicitly used silence-as-consent.

List these as "apparent but unconfirmed agreement" so the follow-up can close them.

### 5. Preserve dissent

If someone disagreed, record it with their name and reason. A decision log that hides dissent is
worse than none, because the disagreement resurfaces later without context.

### 6. Keep it short

Target: decisions ≤ 5 lines each, actions one line each, open questions one line each. The
transcript is the appendix, not the output.

## Rules

- Never attribute a decision to someone who did not make it.
- Never invent a due date. "No date agreed" is a valid and useful entry.
- Never convert a suggestion into an action without an owner.
- Never summarise away a dissent or a risk that was raised.
- Do not include personal or sensitive remarks that are irrelevant to the outcome.
- Do not include side conversations that had no decision or action.

## Output format

```markdown
# <Meeting> — <date>

**Attendees:** <names>
**Duration:** <minutes>

## Decisions
| # | Decision | Decided by | Evidence |
|---|----------|------------|----------|

## Actions
| # | Owner | Action | Due | Done when | Status |
|---|-------|--------|-----|-----------|--------|

## Open questions
- <question> — raised by <name>, needs <person> to resolve

## Apparent but unconfirmed agreement
- "<quote>" — treated as acknowledgement; confirm with <name>

## Dissent and risks recorded
- <name> disagreed with <decision> because <reason>

## Not recorded
- <topic discussed with no outcome>
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Transcript is partial or low quality | Mark gaps explicitly; do not fill from assumption |
| Speaker labels are missing | Use timestamps and quote the text; ask for the attendee list |
| A decision is implied but never stated | Put it in open questions, not decisions |
| Multiple conflicting decisions on one topic | Record both with timestamps and flag the conflict |
| Sensitive HR or legal content | Summarise at the level of "an HR matter was raised"; do not transcribe detail |

## Example

**Input:** 48-minute transcript, six attendees.
**Output:** 3 decisions with named deciders, 7 actions with owners and completion tests, 2 open
questions, and one "sounds good" flagged as unconfirmed rather than counted as approval.

name: dependency-vulnerability-triage
description: Triages reported dependency vulnerabilities into what is actually exploitable in this codebase, what needs an upgrade now, and what can wait, with a reachability check and a safe upgrade path. Use when a scanner produces a long CVE list, when an audit fails CI, or when deciding whether an advisory affects you.
content:
# Dependency Vulnerability Triage

A scanner reports that a vulnerable function exists in your dependency tree. It does not report
that your code calls it. Triage is the work of finding out.

## When to use

- A scanner or audit reports many vulnerabilities.
- CI fails on a security gate.
- A new advisory affects a package you use.
- Deciding between an urgent patch and a scheduled upgrade.

## Workflow

### 1. Establish the real inventory

- Generate an SBOM or a lockfile-derived tree with exact versions.
- Separate **direct** dependencies from **transitive** ones.
- Record whether each is runtime, build-time, or dev-only. A dev-only vulnerability is usually
  not a production risk, though it can be a supply-chain risk.

### 2. For each advisory, answer four questions

| Question | Why it matters |
|----------|----------------|
| Is the vulnerable version actually installed? | Advisories often cover a range you are outside |
| Is the vulnerable code path reachable? | An unused function is not an exploitable path |
| What does exploitation require? | Network access, a specific config, authenticated user, a malicious input |
| Is there a fix, and is it compatible? | An unfixable advisory needs a different response |

Reachability is the key step. A vulnerable XML parser in a transitive dependency that your code
never invokes is low priority; a vulnerable template engine called on every request is urgent.

### 3. Classify

| Priority | Criteria | Response |
|----------|----------|----------|
| P0 | Reachable, remotely exploitable, no auth, fix available | Patch now, out of band |
| P1 | Reachable, requires auth or a specific config | Patch this cycle |
| P2 | Not reachable but easy to make reachable later | Patch in the next scheduled upgrade |
| P3 | Dev-only, or the vulnerable path is unreachable and unlikely to change | Track, document |
| Accepted | No fix, compensating control in place | Record with owner and review date |

### 4. Verify reachability honestly

Ways to check, in order of strength:

1. Search your code for calls to the vulnerable function or its wrapper.
2. Use the dependency's own configuration to see whether the feature is enabled.
3. Run a reachability tool if one is available.
4. If you cannot determine it, classify as P1 rather than P3. Unknown is not safe.

Record the method used. "Not reachable" without evidence is a guess.

### 5. Plan the upgrade

- Prefer the smallest version bump that fixes it; avoid a major upgrade in an emergency unless
  required.
- Check the changelog for breaking changes between your version and the fix.
- If the fix requires a major bump, look for a backport, a patch via a package override, or a
  mitigation.
- Test: run the suite, plus a targeted test of the affected feature.

### 6. Record the decision

For every advisory: status, priority, evidence, action, owner, and date. A triage list that is not
written down is repeated next quarter.

## Rules

- Never mark a vulnerability "not exploitable" without stating how you determined it.
- Never pin to a fork of a package without recording the source and the maintenance plan.
- Never suppress an advisory in the scanner config to make CI pass; record an accepted risk with
  an owner instead.
- Never apply a major upgrade to production without running the test suite.
- Do not paste tokens, internal URLs, or private package registry credentials into a report.

## Output format

```markdown
# Dependency triage – <date>

## Inventory
<package manager, total deps, direct/transitive, runtime/dev>

## Triage
| Advisory | Package | Installed | Fixed in | Reachable? | Evidence | Priority | Action | Owner |

## Urgent actions
1. <package> <current> → <target>, reason, test plan

## Accepted risks
| Advisory | Why accepted | Compensating control | Review date |

## Scanner notes
<any advisory judged a false positive, with evidence>
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| No lockfile or SBOM | Generate one from the package manager before triaging |
| Advisory covers a range with no fix | Look for a backport or mitigation; record as accepted with a review date |
| Package is unmaintained | Treat as a supply-chain risk; propose replacement, do not fork silently |
| Reachability cannot be determined | Classify P1 and say the evidence is missing |
| Scanner reports a vulnerability in a package not in the tree | Verify the scanner's data; mark as a false positive with the command output |

## Example

**Input:** 62 advisories from `npm audit`.
**Output:** 1 P0 (reachable template injection in a direct dependency), 4 P1, 11 P2, 38 P3
(dev-only or unreachable with evidence), 8 accepted with owners; and the exact upgrade path for
the P0 with a targeted test.

name: threat-model-stride
description: Builds a threat model for a system or feature using STRIDE, mapping data flows, trust boundaries, and assets, then ranking threats by realistic impact and producing testable mitigations. Use when designing a new feature, reviewing an architecture, or preparing for a security review.
content:
# Threat Model with STRIDE

A threat model is a list of things that could go wrong, each tied to a specific element and a
specific mitigation you can test.

## When to use

- Designing a feature that handles auth, money, personal data, or file uploads.
- Reviewing an architecture before build.
- Preparing for a security review or a customer questionnaire.
- After an incident, to find the sibling issues.

## Workflow

### 1. Define the scope and the assets

Write down what is in scope and what is not. Then list the assets worth protecting, ranked:

| Asset | Why it matters | Where it lives |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Session tokens | Account takeover | Browser, cookie, server memory |
| Payment records | Financial and legal | Primary DB, backups, logs |
| Uploaded files | Malware, data leak | Object storage, processing workers |

An asset that is not named will not be protected.

### 2. Draw the data flow

Minimal diagram, in text if necessary:

```
[browser] --HTTPS--> [CDN] --> [API gateway] --mTLS--> [service A] --> [DB]
                                              \--> [queue] --> [worker] --> [S3]
```

Mark every **trust boundary**: browser→server, service→service, service→third party,
service→database, admin→production. Threats cluster at boundaries.

### 3. Enumerate threats per element with STRIDE

For each element crossing a boundary, ask all six questions:

| Letter | Threat | Question |
|--------|--------|----------|
| S | Spoofing | Can someone pretend to be another user, service, or the CDN? |
| T | Tampering | Can data be modified in transit, at rest, or in the queue? |
| R | Repudiation | Can an actor deny an action because there is no trustworthy log? |
| I | Information disclosure | Can data leak through errors, logs, timing, or an over-broad response? |
| D | Denial of service | Can one actor exhaust connections, storage, queue depth, or a quota? |
| E | Elevation of privilege | Can a user reach another tenant's data or an admin action? |

Do not stop at the first plausible threat per element. The useful ones are usually the third.

### 4. Rank realistically

Score each threat on:

- **Likelihood:** requires an authenticated user? a leaked token? physical access? a rare race?
- **Impact:** data loss, account takeover, financial loss, reputational, regulatory.
- **Existing controls:** what already prevents or detects it.

Drop threats that require an attacker capability the system already excludes (for example, a
compromised host) unless that assumption is documented and accepted.

### 5. Write testable mitigations

Bad: "Validate input."
Good: "Reject uploads whose declared MIME type is not in {image/png, image/jpeg} AND whose magic
bytes disagree; verify by uploading a `.png` containing PHP and confirming a 415."

Each mitigation needs a verification method: a test, a config check, a query, or a review step.

### 6. Record accepted risks

Some threats will not be fixed. Record them with an owner, a reason, and a review date. An
accepted risk that is written down is a decision; an unrecorded one is an incident waiting.

### 7. Revisit on change

Re-run the model when: a new trust boundary appears, a new data type is stored, auth changes, or
a new third party is added.

## Rules

- Every threat names the element and the boundary it crosses.
- Every mitigation has a verification method.
- Do not list a threat with no plausible path from an attacker position.
- Do not mark a threat "mitigated" without evidence.
- Never include real credentials, tokens, or customer data in the model document.
- Do not rely on "the network is internal" as a control without stating it as an assumption.

## Output format

```markdown
# Threat model: <system / feature>

## Scope
in scope / out of scope / assumptions

## Assets
| Asset | Impact if compromised | Location |

## Data flow and trust boundaries
<diagram or list>

## Threats
| ID | Element | STRIDE | Threat | Likelihood | Impact | Control | Mitigation | Verify by |
|----|---------|--------|--------|------------|--------|---------|------------|-----------|

## Accepted risks
| ID | Risk | Owner | Reason | Review date |

## Open questions
- <question blocking a threat assessment>
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Architecture is unknown | Ask for the data flow; a threat model without boundaries is fiction |
| Threat depends on a control you cannot see | Mark it "assumed controlled — verify" rather than dropping it |
| Scope is the whole company | Narrow to one system; company-wide models become generic checklists |
| User wants only a compliance checklist | Say that a checklist is not a threat model, and offer both |

## Example

**Input:** file-upload feature for customer invoices.
**Output:** 14 threats across 3 boundaries, ranked; the top three are stored-XSS via SVG,
cross-tenant object access through a predictable key, and unbounded decompression; each with a
testable mitigation and a verification step.

name: csv-profiling
description: Profiles a CSV or Parquet dataset before analysis, reporting schema, null rates, cardinality, distributions, duplicate keys, encoding problems, and likely join keys. Use when opening an unfamiliar dataset, when numbers look wrong, or when deciding what cleaning is actually required.
content:
# CSV Profiling

Look at the data before trusting it. Every claim in a later analysis depends on assumptions
this step makes explicit.

## When to use

- First contact with an unfamiliar dataset.
- Totals or counts disagree with another source.
- Deciding which columns can be a key, a category, or a measure.
- Before writing any cleaning code.

## Workflow

### 1. Read the file defensively

- Detect encoding: try UTF-8, then check for a BOM, then Windows-1252. Report which was used.
- Detect the delimiter by counting candidates in the first lines (`,` `;` `\t` `|`).
- Read a 1,000-row sample plus the header before loading everything.
- Note the row count from a full scan; do not assume the sample is representative.

### 2. Profile each column

For every column report:

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `dtype_inferred` | integer, decimal, date, boolean, string, mixed |
| `null_rate` | share of empty or placeholder values (`""`, `NA`, `NULL`, `-`, `n/a`) |
| `distinct` | exact count, and `distinct/null_rows` ratio |
| `min` / `max` / `mean` / `p50` / `p95` | numeric columns only |
| `top_values` | 10 most frequent, with counts |
| `examples` | 3 non-null samples |
| `format_issues` | mixed date formats, thousands separators, currency symbols, trailing spaces |

Placeholders are not nulls. Report them separately: a column that is 40% `"N/A"` strings is
not 40% null, and the difference changes how you clean it.

### 3. Check the shape of the table

- **Duplicates:** exact duplicate rows, and duplicates on the candidate key.
- **Candidate keys:** columns (or combinations) where `distinct == row_count - nulls`. Verify
  uniqueness on the full file, not the sample.
- **Referential sanity:** for ID columns, are there orphan or impossible values?
- **Monotonicity:** is a "date" or "sequence" column actually sorted? Gaps?
- **Constant columns:** zero variance — usually a broken export, not a feature.

### 4. Check numeric plausibility

- Negative values in a count or quantity column.
- Percentages outside 0–100.
- Amounts with more decimal places than the currency allows.
- Extreme outliers: report the top and bottom 5 values with row numbers. Do not remove them
  in profiling; removal is a later, explicit decision.

### 5. Check dates and time zones

- Confirm the format by parsing, not by eyeballing.
- Identify whether timestamps carry an offset. If not, state the assumed zone.
- Check for the "midnight default" pattern: many rows at exactly 00:00:00 usually means a date
  was coerced into a timestamp.

### 6. Report

Produce `PROFILE.md` plus a machine-readable `profile.json`. Lead with the five findings that
would most likely invalidate an analysis.

## Rules

- Never modify the source file. Profiling is read-only.
- Never infer a key from column names alone; verify uniqueness on the full data.
- Report mixed types explicitly; do not silently coerce a column to string.
- Do not drop outliers during profiling.
- State the exact row count profiled and whether it was a sample.

## Output format

```markdown
# Profile: <file>
Rows: 1,284,002 | Columns: 27 | Encoding: UTF-8 (BOM) | Delimiter: ,

## Headline findings
1. `customer_id` has 412 duplicate values — not a unique key.
2. `amount` is 3.1% empty strings, not nulls.
3. `created_at` is 38% exactly midnight — likely date-only source.
4. `country` has 14 spellings of 4 countries.
5. `qty` has 6 negative values, all on cancelled orders.

## Columns
| column | type | null% | distinct | notes |
...

## Cleaning required before analysis
- <specific step, with the column and the rule>
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| File too large to load in memory | Profile in chunks; compute exact distinct counts with a set or a probabilistic sketch, and say which |
| Ragged rows (wrong field count) | Report the line numbers and the expected vs actual count; do not guess at a fix |
| Binary content in a text file | Detect and report; refuse to parse |
| No header row | Report the inferred header and ask for confirmation before continuing |

## Example

**Input:** `orders.csv`, 1.28M rows.
**Output:** profile with 5 headline findings, a column table, and a cleaning list of 7 items —
duplicate `customer_id`, three date formats, a currency-symbol amount column, and 412 rows
with a negative quantity on non-cancelled orders.

name: address-normalization
description: Normalises messy postal addresses into a canonical form, geocodes them with a confidence score, and routes low-confidence matches to manual review instead of silently guessing. Use when cleaning a customer or delivery address list, matching addresses across systems, or preparing data for routing.
content:
# Address Normalization

An address pipeline that reports its own uncertainty. A wrong geocode is worse than a missing
one, because it looks correct downstream.

## When to use

- Cleaning an address list before geocoding or delivery.
- Matching the same address across two systems.
- Preparing delivery stops for routing.
- Auditing a list where deliveries failed.

## Workflow

### 1. Understand the input distribution

Profile the column first: how many are free-text, how many already have components, which
countries, and what the common malformations are. Sample 30 rows by hand and note the patterns
before writing rules.

### 2. Normalise in layers

Apply in order, recording which layer changed each row:

| Layer | Action |
|-------|--------|
| Encoding | Fix mojibake, normalise Unicode (NFKC), strip control characters |
| Whitespace | Collapse runs, trim, remove trailing punctuation |
| Case | Title-case for display; keep a case-folded copy for matching |
| Abbreviations | `St` → `Street`, `Rd` → `Road`, `Apt`/`#`/`Unit` → a single unit field |
| Directionals | `N` → `North`, applied per country convention |
| Country names | Map to ISO 3166-1 alpha-2; record the mapping used |
| Subdivision | Map to ISO 3166-2 where the country has them |
| Postal code | Apply the country's pattern; reject impossible lengths |
| Phone-like noise | Remove stray phone numbers, emails, and delivery notes from the address field |

Never apply US-centric rules to a non-US address. Detect the country first; if unknown, keep
the original and mark it for review.

### 3. Parse into components

Target: `line1, line2, locality, admin_area, postal_code, country`. Use a parser appropriate to
the country rather than one global regex. Where parsing is ambiguous, keep the original string
alongside the parsed parts — never discard the source.

### 4. Geocode with explicit confidence

Record per address:

| Field | Example |
|-------|---------|
| `match_type` | exact / interpolated / street-centroid / locality-centroid / no-match |
| `confidence` | 0–1, from the provider plus your own checks |
| `provider` | which service returned it |
| `lat`, `lon` | coordinates |
| `precision` | rooftop / parcel / street / city |

**Reject anything at locality-centroid precision for delivery.** A city-level geocode is fine
for mapping a customer base and useless for routing.

### 5. Add independent validation

Do not rely on one provider. Cross-check:

- Postal code is consistent with the city and state.
- Coordinates fall inside the country polygon.
- Two providers agree within ~100 m for rooftop claims.
- The building number exists on the matched street where the provider supports it.

Disagreement is a review flag, not a reason to average the coordinates.

### 6. Route to review

Buckets:

- `auto_accept` — exact match, high confidence, all checks pass.
- `review` — interpolated, provider disagreement, or a corrected component.
- `reject` — no match, or impossible combination.

Report counts per bucket and per country. A 30% review rate is a finding about the input, not a
failure of the pipeline.

## Rules

- Never invent a missing component (postal code, city) to make a match succeed.
- Never overwrite the original address; keep it in `source_address`.
- Never discard a failed geocode; it belongs in the review bucket.
- Respect provider terms of service and caching restrictions.
- Do not store coordinates for addresses you are not permitted to process.

## Output format

```
normalized.csv
  source_address, line1, line2, locality, admin_area, postal_code, country,
  lat, lon, match_type, confidence, precision, bucket, provider, changed_layers
REVIEW.md   # counts by bucket and country, top failure patterns, examples
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Country cannot be determined | Keep the original, bucket `review`, do not assume |
| Provider returns multiple candidates | Choose only if one is clearly closer; otherwise `review` with candidates listed |
| Rate limited | Back off, cache results, and resume; never switch to an unauthorised provider |
| Address is a PO box or military address | Tag it; do not attempt street-level geocoding |

## Example

**Input:** 8,400 customer addresses, mostly UK and Ireland.
**Output:** 71% auto-accept, 24% review, 5% reject; the review list dominated by addresses with
a missing postcode and by 60 rows where two providers disagreed by more than 2 km.

name: route-optimization
description: Builds and validates a multi-stop route plan from a list of locations, time windows, vehicle capacity, and driver constraints, then explains why the solver's answer is or is not trustworthy. Use when planning deliveries, service visits, or field work, or when a route plan looks wrong.
content:
# Route Optimization

Optimisation without validation produces confident nonsense. This skill defines the problem,
solves it, then checks the answer against reality.

## When to use

- Planning daily deliveries or service visits with more than ~8 stops.
- Comparing a proposed plan against the current manual route.
- Diagnosing a plan that assigns an impossible sequence.
- Adding time windows or capacity to an existing plan.

## Workflow

### 1. Define the problem completely

A route problem is under-specified until all of these are answered:

| Element | Question |
|---------|----------|
| Depot | Where does each route start and end? |
| Stops | Coordinates, service duration, demand |
| Vehicles | How many, capacity per dimension, fixed and per-km cost |
| Time windows | Per stop; hard or soft? |
| Drivers | Shift start/end, mandatory breaks, max driving hours |
| Travel model | Straight-line, road network, or a traffic-aware matrix |
| Objective | Minimise distance, time, cost, or lateness? In what priority? |
| Constraints | One-way streets, access restrictions, vehicle height/weight, customer preferences |

If any of these is missing, state the assumption explicitly and mark the plan provisional.

### 2. Get a travel-time matrix, not distances

Use a routing provider's matrix for the actual road network. Straight-line distance
underestimates travel by 30–60% in cities and produces plans that are impossible to drive.

Cache the matrix. A 200-stop problem is 40,000 pairs; recomputing per solver iteration is slow
and expensive.

### 3. Choose the solver by size

| Stops | Approach |
|-------|----------|
| ≤ 10 | Exact (brute force or dynamic programming) |
| 11–50 | Heuristic: nearest neighbour + 2-opt, or OR-Tools with a time limit |
| 51–500 | OR-Tools with guided local search, time-limited |
| > 500 | Cluster first (geographic sectors), then solve per cluster |

Always report the solver's gap or whether it hit the time limit. "Optimal" is a claim that
requires proof.

### 4. Model the constraints that actually bind

- **Time windows:** hard windows produce infeasible problems quickly. Report infeasibility and
  the minimum relaxation needed (which window, by how many minutes) rather than silently
  dropping stops.
- **Capacity:** track every dimension (weight, volume, count), not just one.
- **Driving hours:** insert breaks and enforce daily limits.
- **Service time:** include it; a 15-minute stop × 40 stops is 10 hours.

### 5. Validate the output against the physical world

Before presenting a plan:

- Every stop appears exactly once.
- Sequence respects every time window and break.
- Capacity is not exceeded on any leg.
- Total driving time is within legal limits.
- No leg is implausibly fast (implies a bad matrix entry).
- Compare against the naive baseline: current manual route, or nearest-neighbour. Report the
  improvement as a percentage, not an absolute claim.

### 6. Present with the assumptions

A route plan is only as good as its inputs. State: matrix source and timestamp, traffic model,
assumed service times, and which constraints were relaxed.

## Rules

- Never present a plan as "optimal" without a proven optimality gap of zero.
- Never drop a stop to make the problem feasible; report infeasibility.
- Never use straight-line distance for a plan that will actually be driven, unless the user
  explicitly accepts the approximation.
- Never average coordinates for a multi-stop location; use a real access point.
- Respect provider terms for matrix and geocoding usage.

## Output format

```markdown
# Route plan: <date> – <fleet>

## Assumptions
depot, matrix source and time, traffic model, service times, objective and priority

## Result
| Route | Vehicle | Stops | Distance | Driving | Service | Window violations |
|-------|---------|-------|----------|---------|---------|-------------------|

## Sequence
Route 1: depot → stop 14 (08:05–08:20) → stop 3 (08:41–08:56) → ... → depot (17:10)

## Validation
- all stops assigned: yes
- capacity respected: yes
- windows respected: yes, 0 violations
- driving hours within limit: yes
- improvement vs baseline: −18% distance, −11% time

## Not satisfied / relaxed
- <constraint> — reason and impact
```

## Error handling

| Condition | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Problem is infeasible | Report which constraint set conflicts, and the smallest relaxation that makes it feasible |
| Matrix provider rate-limited | Use cached entries; report coverage; do not substitute straight-line silently |
| Solver hits its time limit | Report the gap and the best solution found; label it "not proven optimal" |
| Stop coordinates are low precision | Flag them; a city-centroid stop invalidates the leg times |

## Example

**Input:** 62 deliveries, 4 vans, 08:00–17:00 windows, 20-minute service, London.
**Output:** a 4-route plan, 0 window violations, −18% distance versus the manual route, a note
that two stops are only city-precision and may add 10 minutes each, and the exact matrix
timestamp used.
